newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea workers rally to protest over labour law.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea workers rally to protest over labour law.

text.p: South Korea's unionised workers and students staged rallies in major cities including Seoul on Saturday as they stepped up their protests against a controversial new labour law, witnesses said.
Some 5,000 protesters gathered at Seoul's Myungdong Cathedral before marching through the streets demanding the suspension of the law, one witness said.
Anti-government rallies were also reported in Pusan, Inchon and other cities.

The nation's two union unbrella groups threatened earlier on Saturday to step up industrial action until the government repeals the law, which gives employers the right to lay off employees, hire temporary workers and replace strikers.
"The law is designed to kill democracy and human rights," Kwon Young-kil, chairman of the outlawed Korea Confederation of Trade Unions, told reporters.
The government argues that changes in the law would benefit unions and employers by creating a more flexible labour market.

Kwon said about 200 unions at the nation's major car makers, ship builders, other manufacturers and secondary financial institutions, representing some 230,000 members, would go strike from Monday morning.

"From Tuesday, unionised workers at subway, hospitals and broadcasting companies will join in the work stoppage. We have also proposed cooperating with the Federation of Korean Trade Unions," Kwon said.
The two umbrella union groups between them claim a total membership of 1.7 million in most of South Korea's major industries and public-sector services.
Nationwide strikes erupted on December 26 after the ruling New Korea Party pushed through the new labour law during a clandestine session of parliament.
The stoppages, which hit car and ship production, hospitals and subways, were suspended until after the New Year holidays in a goodwill gesture to the public.

A strike call last Friday by the Korea Confederation of Trade Unions received a mixed response. While the organisers said some 96,000 workers at 46 unions answered its call, the Labour Ministry estimated that some 22,800 workers out of 31 unions were involved.
The number of striking workers dropped by half on Saturday because many companies extended the New Year holidays until Sunday, the confederation said.
Fears of labour unrest continued to hurt the nation's stock market, with the Seoul bourse falling to a 45-month low by the end of Saturday's half-day session.
The composite index fell 10.38 points to 643.41, the lowest since March 16, 1993, when it ended at 637.87.
"Labour unrest is expected to flare up again from Monday. That expectation prompted selling of shares," said Kim Heung-shik, a broker at Hyundai Securities.

The more moderate Federation of Korean Trade Unions, the nation's largest union group, has also announced it plans a large-scale rally on January 10 and a general strike by all of its members a day later.
The body said its second round of strikes would be led by unions in the public and service sectors.
"I hope the government does not underestimate our will to fight," said a federation spokesman.
